name: Hartwig Museum / in formation
desc: A museum taking shape around the production of new work.
question: Can a museum be a set of conditions before it is a destination?
text: Hartwig’s future museum is planned to open in 2028. Its programme joins exhibition spaces with places for artists to work, stay, and exchange. Acquisitions are to be donated to the Dutch state collection rather than retained as the museum’s own collection.
context: The host’s institutional experiment makes the cultivation question concrete: what must a museum provide so that artistic work can begin and continue?
criteriaNote: The museum building is being transformed. Public access is marked “no” for the future museum venue, not for the foundation’s current activities or Hartwig Proxy.

name: ZKM | Center for Art and Media
desc: A museum that also researches, develops, and produces.
question: What if a museum’s medium is the work it makes possible?
text: ZKM brings research and production together with exhibitions, performances, collections, and archives. Its laboratories create new work and address the technical challenge of preserving media art.
context: Artistic R&D requires tools, collaborators, and maintenance. ZKM makes those supporting conditions part of the institution itself.
criteriaNote: Public access includes programmed exhibitions; it does not imply free admission.

name: Rubin Museum of Himalayan Art
place: Distributed / originating in New York, USA
desc: A museum continuing beyond a single physical home.
question: If the building goes away, where does the museum live?
text: The Rubin has evolved into a global museum without a singular physical space. It works through travelling exhibitions, partnerships, participatory experiences, digital resources, and support for artists and scholars.
context: Here, the museum persists through a collection, relationships, and a mission. A devotional field of attention travels beyond one address.
criteriaNote: Public access includes programmed exhibitions; it does not imply free admission.

name: Museum of Witchcraft and Magic
desc: Objects and records of magical belief and practice.
question: Can an institution exhibit a practice without neutralising its power?
text: The museum preserves objects, books, and archival material connected to magical practice. Its collection makes room for forms of knowledge often treated as peripheral to institutional authority.
context: A devotional turn raises a curatorial problem: what happens to an object of belief when it becomes an object of observation?
criteriaNote: Public access includes programmed exhibitions; it does not imply free admission.

name: Inhotim
desc: Contemporary art and a botanical garden in the same field of attention.
question: What changes when some of the collection is alive?
text: Inhotim combines a contemporary art museum and botanical garden. Its plant collections are accompanied by environmental education, conservation, and research. Artworks and living systems ask for different kinds of care in a shared landscape.
context: The programme’s concern with plant worlds becomes an institutional question: can a museum make room for forms of life that grow beyond its categories?
criteriaNote: Public access includes programmed exhibitions; it does not imply free admission.

name: Bethlem Museum of the Mind
desc: Art, archives, and objects in the grounds of a working hospital.
question: Whose inner life becomes visible—and who interprets it?
text: Situated at Bethlem Royal Hospital, the museum cares for art, archives, and historic objects connected to mental healthcare. Its collections offer ways of approaching lived experience alongside institutional history.
context: A conversation about consciousness also needs to ask who is authorised to describe another person’s experience.
criteriaNote: Public access includes programmed exhibitions; it does not imply free admission.

name: Te Papa Tongarewa
desc: A national museum built through relationships with communities.
question: Who has the authority to care for a collection?
text: Te Papa describes itself as a bicultural national museum. Its work includes relationships with iwi and a programme to return Māori and Moriori ancestral remains. Keeping can also involve returning.
context: Care for a collection can require giving things back. Interrelation changes what ownership can mean.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: District Six Museum
desc: A place to work with the memory of a displaced community.
question: Can a museum help a community re-member itself?
text: Before opening its permanent exhibition in 1994, the museum worked as a travelling movement, creating collecting points and spaces for storytelling. Former residents remain central to its work of memory and restitution.
context: An institution can form through relationships and practices before it acquires a permanent exhibition space.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: Museum of Jurassic Technology
desc: A museum that makes the act of believing feel strange.
question: Can a museum make uncertainty its subject?
text: Its presentation borrows the authority of a museum while inviting you to question how that authority works.
context: The devotional question is also a question of authority: what makes us trust a display, a label, or a voice?
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: Chichu Art Museum
desc: Art, architecture, and daylight, mostly beneath the earth.
question: When the building is an artwork, what is the museum?
text: Built largely underground, Chichu brings works by Claude Monet, James Turrell, and Walter De Maria into a building designed by Tadao Ando. Natural light changes the encounter throughout the day.
context: Presence changes with light, duration, and the body moving through space. The encounter is part of the work.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: Sulabh International Museum of Toilets
desc: The history of sanitation, brought into view.
question: Who decided which objects deserved a pedestal?
text: Founded in 1992 by Bindeshwar Pathak, this museum uses objects, pictures, and historical material to trace the development of sanitation.
context: Institutions train attention. A history of sanitation asks whose daily needs are made visible, and whose are omitted.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: Museum of Obsolete Media
desc: Preserving the things that once held our memories.
question: Does a collection need to let you through the door?
text: Jason Curtis’s physical collection underpins a virtual museum launched in 2013. The physical collection is not open to the public; its catalogue can be explored online. Here, “public access” includes online access, while “a building” means a dedicated visitor museum.
context: Artistic R&D has a maintenance problem: the media that store a work may outlive the machines that make it perceptible.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: Museo Nacional del Prado
desc: A royal collection becomes a public way of seeing.
question: How does private taste become public heritage?
text: The Prado’s collection owes much to the collecting tastes of Spanish monarchs. Its history makes a familiar museum form feel contingent: someone’s choices become an institution’s inheritance.
context: Every collection embodies choices. The institutional question is how those choices become a public inheritance.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: Museum of Broken Relationships
desc: Ordinary objects carrying the weight of an ending.
question: Can the story turn an ordinary object into an exhibit?
text: Objects donated by members of the public are exhibited with the stories of the relationships they recall. The collection gives personal experiences a shared space.
context: Care can start with something too private, too ordinary, or too painful for a conventional collection.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: The Museum of Innocence
desc: A novel and a museum, imagined together.
question: Can a fictional life leave a real collection?
text: Orhan Pamuk developed his novel and museum together. Display cabinets contain the everyday things his fictional characters used, saw, and dreamed of. The museum opened in 2012.
context: A constructed world can change how we attend to actual objects. Fiction becomes a device for producing presence.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: A grandmother’s kitchen
desc: Recipes, rituals, utensils. A collection kept in use.
question: Must preservation stop a thing from being used?
text: Imagine a kitchen where knowledge passes through gestures, meals, and familiar objects. It has a collection and a place, but no public opening hours. This is a proposed boundary case, not a documented institution.
context: A hypothetical test of devotion as repeated attention: can a practice of everyday care constitute a museum?
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: A seed library
desc: A collection whose survival depends on being planted.
question: Can a museum preserve by giving its collection away?
text: Imagine a publicly accessible seed collection that circulates through a community, without a dedicated museum building. Its objects change, multiply, and return. This hypothetical case asks whether permanence is the right test.
context: A hypothetical living collection. Cultivation would preserve its future by letting it change.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: The internet
desc: An archive without a single curator or a stable edge.
question: Is everything saved also something remembered?
text: Consider the internet as an accidental collection. Publicly accessible in part, dispersed across infrastructure, with no single museum building or coherent collection of physical exhibits. This framing is a provocation, not a claim that the internet is an accredited museum.
context: A hypothetical test of scale: storage alone offers no guarantee of care, context, or continued access.
criteriaNote: “Building” means a dedicated museum venue, not simply any structure. Public access may be physical or online; it does not imply free admission.

name: Museu do Amanhã
desc: Science, art, and possible futures brought into the present.
question: Can a museum collect questions about what has not happened?
text: The Museum of Tomorrow describes its purpose through the meeting of science, art, and innovation: exploring the present and imagining the future.
context: A museum can direct attention forward. The presence it cultivates may be responsibility toward lives and worlds that do not yet exist.
criteriaNote: Physical objects have not been classified here. Unknown means unassessed, not absent.
